newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Conrail, CSX say would meet rival. [CORRECTED 19:51 GMT]
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Conrail, CSX say would meet rival. [CORRECTED 19:51 GMT]

text.p: In what may be a break in the three-month takeover battle for Conrail Inc., Conrail and CSX Corp. said Wednesday they would be willing to meet with rival Norfolk Southern Corp. to discuss the battle.
The heads of Conrail and CSX Corp. said in a letter to Norfolk Southern Corp. Chairman David Goode they would be willing to hold "meaningful and candid discussions" without preconditions.

The letter, sent in response to a letter from Goode on Tuesday calling for talks, said Philadelphia-based Conrail and Richmond, Va.-based CSX remained "fully committed" to their merger and that a meeting should not be interpreted as a change in position by either side.
A copy of the letter was provided to Reuters.

A meeting of the three sides would be the first in the course of the three-month takeover battle for Conrail, in which Norfolk Southern is seeking to break up the proposed CSX-Conrail merger and acquire Conrail for itself.
A Norfolk Southern spokesman called the response from Conrail and CSX a "positive development."
He said Goode and CSX Chairman John Snow had spoken briefly by telephone late Wednesday afternoon but no date had been set for a meeting.
(Deletes reference to Conrail chairman David LeVan).
"We appreciate their prompt response and we regard it as a positive development," said Norfolk Southern spokesman Bob Fort.
Norfolk, Va.-based Norfolk Southern has offered $10.3 billion cash for Conrail, which has agreed to a cash-and-stock deal with CSX now worth about $9.5 billion.
Conrail shareholders Friday signaled their dissatisfaction with the CSX deal by rejecting a change to the company charter that would have let the deal proceed.

Norfolk Southern on Wednesday launched a tender offer to buy 9.9 percent of Conrail stock -- the largest stake it could hold without triggering a Conrail "poison pill" anti-takeover provision -- for $115 cash per share.

A Wall Street takeover stock trader said the exchange of letters may signal movement toward a settlement of the takeover battle, or may represent just public relations maneuvering. "Usually, you start talking, something happens (but) this one has not followed any notion of a script," he said.

In their letter, Levan and Snow told Goode: "We are fully committed to the CSX/Conrail merger. We believe our merger, together with your participation, will enable us to best serve the interests of all our constituencies, preserve our merger synergies and yield a pro-competitive result."

"We recognize that you have a different view of our merger; nevertheless we should ... meet and talk. This can and should be done without any preconditions that would limit our discussions or otherwise prejudice our respective positions," they said.

"Let us be very clear, no one should interpret from our meeting that either party has changed its position. Our objective, which we are sure you share, is to assure that the public's interest in strong, viable competition is met. We want no winner or loser, other than to be sure that the public is a winner," the CSX and Conrail letter said.
The two chairmen said they looked forward to meeting Goode at "his earliest possible convenience."

Goode said in his letter Tuesday that Norfolk Southern would enter talks conditional on a "recognition" that it had pledged to Conrail shareholders that it would only enter into an agreement with Conrail and CSX that gave Conrail shareholders an all-cash offer of $115 per share, the amount of Norfolk Southern's bid.
